issues.title: Find a better name for the scheme
issues.author: kkohbrok
issues.body: So far we've called the scheme subgroups and virtual clients. The former clashes with RFC9420 ("Subgroup branching") and the latter is quite abstract and a bit too technical. Other options include "Multi-client" or "Multi-device", but that may be a bit generic, as there are other ways to use MLS with multiple clients/devices.

comments.author: Bren2010
comments.body: I actually really like the name virtual clients!

issues.title: Adopt reuse guard approach
issues.author: kkohbrok
issues.body:
Prior to adoption, we agreed that we wanted to switch to an approach where the reuse of nonces is prevented by the reuse guard. Adopting that approach also means that the number of emulating clients is limited.

The draft needs to be adapted to reflect that.

issues.title: Truncate PPRF input and nodes to 32 bytes for larger hash functions?
issues.author: kkohbrok
issues.body: The PPRF is already quite large with 32 bytes per node. Ciphersuites with larger hash function outputs unnecessarily make it even larger.

comments.author: kkohbrok
comments.body: This was solved by the switch to a SecretTree-style PPRF with a tree size corresponding to the RatchetTree of the emulation group.

issues.title: What are generation IDs?
issues.author: Bren2010
issues.body:
I'm confused about the purpose of this feature. It requires passing the group ID, epoch, generation, and ratchet type into a PRF with a secret key. But everything going into the PRF (except the secret key) is all public information. So what purpose does the PRF serve?

/cc @kkohbrok

comments.author: kkohbrok
comments.body:
TL;DR: It's to allow the DS to avoid storing the actual generation because that leaks activity metadata in the state-snapshot adversary model.

The DS has to persist some sort of information to detect duplicate use of individual ratchet generations of any virtual client. The emulator client sending a private message through a virtual client could just send the actual ratchet generation, but that would leak the number of messages sent by the virtual client in that particular epoch. Using pseudorandom generation IDs prevents that.

Of course the DS can always observe and count the number of messages. What this is trying to prevent is leakage in the threat model where an adversary only has access to state snapshots, but doesn't otherwise have visibility into network traffic.

pulls.title: flesh out emulation client onboarding procedure
pulls.author: kkohbrok

comments.body: Why does the joining emulator client have to send its own commit? Would be preferable for it not to
I think there's supposed to be a new header here separating trade-offs from the protocol definitions

Good point. I initially thought it would be easier for the adder to provide the new client only with the group state necessary to create a commit (upon which it could derive the remaining secrets in the new epoch). But it turns out the new client needs pretty much all possible secrets to do that. So you're right, it's not necessary to do a commit at that point.

If the new client doesn't update, we may run into trouble regarding the `reuse_guard` computation.

Both the number of emulator clients in a group and their leaf index go into the compuation of the `reuse_guard`. If we allow those two to change while the higher-level epoch stays the same, we run the risk of nonce collisions.

Consider the following scenario:

- There are two emulator clients (1 and 2) emulating a virtual client in group X
- Emulator client 2 sends a message in group X at ratchet generation 0 (which emulator client 1 never receives)
- Emulator client 1 removes emulator client 2
- Emulator client 1 adds emulator client 3 and transfers all of its group state
- Emulator client 3 now occupies the same leaf index as previously emulator client 2
- Emulator client 3 now sends a message into group X at ratchet generation 0

At the time emulator client 2 and emulator client 3 send their messages, they use the same `prp_key`, the emulator group is the same size and they occupy the same leaf index in the emulator group. The security of the message thus rests entirely on how random `x` really is.

All in all, I think it's safer if we mandate that the new client doesn't send any messages in groups until the virtual client has been updated in that group.

Since the reuse_guard computation is essentially bound to a certain configuration of the emulator group, maybe it makes sense to derive it once per emulation group epoch and then use it across all higher-level groups that use secrets derived from that epoch. That would make bookkeeping easier for implementations.

> Emulator client 1 removes emulator client 2

This step would require rotating the leaf in the supergroup, which would change the computation of the reuse_guard.

I could still see this being an issue though if we have emulator 1 and 2 in an emulation group, and then emulator 2 adds emulator 3. Because emulator 2 and 3 will be generating x's that are = 1 or 2 mod 3, while emulator 1 will be generating x's that are = 0 mod 2 until it learns about emulator 3.

Saying that a supergroup's LeafNode needs to be from the most recent emulator group epoch before you send a message seems like a good solution, yes.

pulls.title: smaller PPRF design
pulls.author: kkohbrok
pulls.body: This PR replaces the rather large 32-byte input PPRF for operation secrets with an RFC9420-style SecretTree + per-leaf Ratchet construction. This changes slightly how operation secrets are derived, but makes the PPRF significantly smaller.

comments.author: kkohbrok
comments.body:
> I went over it and it makes a lot of sense.
> 
> Just leaving a note, no strong opinions: Have you considered a separate ratchet for each operation type? This assumes a fixed set of operation types. On the other hand, it may optimize storage. So for example say a client has leaf node operations interleaved with key package operations and it deletes the secrets for leaf node operations. With one ratchet per operation type it could store just the beginning of the key package ratchet.

Good idea. I don't think it necessarily assumes a fixed set of operations. When the client needs a secret for an operation, it either uses an existing ratchet, or spawns a new one for the operation type. Then we make ratchet spawning generic for the operation type.

So for example say a client has leaf node operations interleaved with key package operations and it deletes the secrets for leaf node operations. With one ratchet per operation type it could store just the beginning of the key package ratchet.

pulls.title: derive `reuse_guard_secret` secret from epoch base secret
pulls.author: kkohbrok
pulls.body:
(Stacked on #17)

This PR has clients derive the `reuse_guard_secret` from the `emulator_epoch_secret`. This changes its scope from per-higher-level group to per-emulation group epoch. This shouldn't impact security, but reduces the amount of bookkeeping for implementations.

reviews.author: mulmarta
reviews.body: So for my understanding, you're saying that deriving one `reuse_guard_secret` per higher level group is an overkill, because we don't need to guard against key reuse between groups. These groups already have different key schedules, so AEAD keys and nonces will be different. It makes sense to me.

comments.body: note: `random` will change after #17
Good point. I'll keep that in mind when merging.

pulls.title: Provide more explanation of generation ids
pulls.author: Bren2010

comments.body:
I believe this would violate the MUST of [9420's deletion schedule](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9420.html#name-deletion-schedule).

> It is important to delete all security-sensitive values as soon as they are consumed. A sensitive value S is said to be consumed if:
>
>   - S was used to encrypt or (successfully) decrypt a message, or a key, nonce, or secret derived from S has been consumed. (This goes for values derived via DeriveSecret as well as ExpandWithLabel.)
>
>Here S may be the init_secret, commit_secret, epoch_secret, or encryption_secret as well as any secret in a secret tree or one of the ratchets.
>
>As soon as a group member consumes a value, they MUST immediately delete (all representations of) that value.

That may be okay, but we should at least make that clear here.
